name: Kundalakarneswarar Temple, Tirukkurakkukka
deity: Shiva as Kundalakarneswarar (Kundaleswarar), with the goddess Kundalambikai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); a small village temple with later renewals
summary: Kundalakarneswarar is the Shiva temple of Thirukurakkaval praised by Appar in the Tevaram as Tirukkurakkukka, loved above all for the tradition that the monkey-god Hanuman worshipped the Lord here and offered his own earring.

sections.history: Thirukurakkaval lies in the old Chola country north of the Kaveri, a short distance from Vaitheeswaran Koil in present-day Mayiladuthurai district. In the Tevaram hymns the shrine is Tirukkurakkukka, and it is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams, praised by the saint Appar, Tirunavukkarasar. Tradition numbers it the twenty-eighth of the Tevaram shrines on the Kaveri's northern bank, and local accounts speak of a sanctuary well over a thousand years old, though its structural history is not firmly documented. The place is remembered less for a royal foundation than for a devotion: the Lord here is said to have been worshipped by Hanuman himself, and the very name of the town is read in that light.
sections.architecture: This is a modest village temple rather than a monumental one, and accounts note that it has no towering rajagopuram. The sanctum holds Shiva as Kundalakarneswarar, also called Kundaleswarar, whose linga tradition describes as one fashioned of sand, and the goddess Kundalambikai is honoured in a shrine of her own. The temple's sacred water is the Ganapathy Theertham, spoken of as a channel of the Kaveri. Hanuman, shown at worship before Shiva, is the figure with whom the place is most closely linked, and some devotees know it as the temple of Anjaneya, the devotee of Shiva. The older stonework is thinly recorded, so come expecting a quiet, simple sanctuary rather than a grand complex.
sections.legends: The temple's story is Hanuman's. After the war in Lanka, Rama is said to have asked him to bring a Shiva linga from Ayodhya; when he was delayed a sand linga was made, and a divine voice then directed Hanuman to install a linga of his own at this place and pray to it. To test his devotion, Shiva made one of his earrings, the kundalam, vanish, and Hanuman, who was born with earrings, cut off one of his own and offered it to the Lord. From this the Lord is called Kundalakarneswarar, He of the earring. A local reading takes the town's name from kurangu, the monkey, as if Kurangukkaa had softened into Kurakkukka, and it is told that two monkeys still come in the month of Chithirai to worship with bilva leaves. These are tradition and local belief, held with affection.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in February or March is the great night of worship here, and Tirukarthikai in November or December is kept with lamps. Hanuman Jayanti has a special place at a temple so closely tied to Hanuman's devotion, and Chithirai, in April or May, is remembered for the belief in the monkeys' annual visit. Monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thirukurakkaval is a place for a slow, quiet visit. Come to the sanctum of Kundalakarneswarar first, then to the goddess Kundalambikai in her own shrine, and spend a moment where Hanuman is shown at worship, remembering the earring offered in love. The temple stands among fields and village lanes, far from the bustle of the highway towns, and many pilgrims fit it into a half-day circuit from Vaitheeswaran Koil with the nearby Tevaram shrines of Tiruvazhkolipputhur, Tirukkaruppariyalur and Tirupunkur.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the late afternoon and evening, with a midday break; village temples keep short hours, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirukurakkaval is a village about 13 km north of Mayiladuthurai and close to Vaitheeswaran Koil, which has the nearest railway station; Mayiladuthurai Junction is the main railhead. Buses run to Vaitheeswaran Koil, from where an auto-rickshaw or taxi covers the last stretch. Tiruchirappalli has the nearest major airport, a few hours away by road.
